attributes.title: Level 6

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the paint tool to create an outline of a forward facing sprite image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might you space out pixels in the paint editor to draw the head of the person sprite?

❓ How might you space out pixels in the paint editor to draw the body of the person sprite?

❓ What other features should be included in a pixel art outline of a person sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Brainstorm with the ninja the general shape of the person sprite outline. Have them consider whether the head should be perfectly round, or more of an irregular shape. Prompt them to consider what other features (e.g. arms, legs, ears) should be clearly shown in the sprite’s outline.

💡 If a ninja is having trouble drawing a person sprite outline, encourage them to look at premade sprites in the gallery to gain a sense of how MakeCode has outlined their sprites.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by drawing the outline of a forward facing person image. 


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen. Create a new spriteForward image asset, then use the paint tool to draw an outline of a person sprite using black pixels. 


Try out different sizes for the head to body ratio and notice how that changes the way the sprite appears. Notice how the proportions may not match how people look realistically, but will look good on screen.  


The sprite outline might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you consider how much of the head should be covered by hair, and how much of the sprite’s face should be shown?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What colors might be used for the sprite’s hair and face?

❓ What other features might you draw on the sprite’s face?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use any color in the color palette to fill in the sprite’s outline; they do not have to conform to realistic hair and skin colors. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to play with the spacing of the different colors on the sprite’s face. They may fill in the base color of the face first, then add hair and tinker with how much space the hair takes up. Have the ninja think through how they might add eyes, a nose, and/or a mouth to the sprite’s face (keeping the size of the pixels in mind).
steps.instructions:
Draw the details of the person sprite’s face.


Use the paint tool to fill in the outline of the head with base colors for the hair and face. Select a color to be used for the face, and another color for the hair. The outline of the head may need to be adjusted after changes to the hairstyle.


Add facial features to the head, such as eyes using a white pixel below a pixel of another color.


The sprite’s face might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you use complementary or analogous colors to add details to the body of the forward facing sprite image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might you use complementary and/or analogous colors to add clothing to the sprite’s outline?

❓ How might you use different colors to separate each part of the sprite’s body?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to brainstorm what type of clothing they might add to the sprite’s body and what colors might pair well together (either to blend naturally or create a contrast). 

💡Remind the ninja that complementary colors are colors opposite each other on the color wheel, which can be used to enhance contrast in an image. Analogous colors are near each other on the color wheel, or in MakeCode’s color palette, and have similar colors. Using analogous colors can help ease a transition from one color to the next in an image.
steps.instructions:
Draw the details of the person sprite’s body.


Use the paint tool to fill in the outline of the body with base colors for clothes. Select colors for the clothes that match the theme of the sprite, and adjust the outline as needed so the style of the clothes fit the character. 


Use the same color used for the face for any skin shown on the body, such as the hands. The outline of the body may need to be adjusted after changes to the clothes, arms, or other parts of the person sprite’s shape.


The sprite’s body might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you consider what the sprite will look like from behind, and update the head and body to fit?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What should appear the same on the back of the sprite’s body? What should appear differently?

❓ Why might it be useful to have an image showing a different perspective of a sprite’s body?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the ninja is struggling to think about what might be similar/different on the back of the sprite’s body, encourage them to look at premade backward-facing sprites in the gallery to gain a sense of how MakeCode has shown this perspective.

💡 Remind the ninja that in top-down games, the user’s perspective is from above the sprite, meaning that they should be able to see all sides of a sprite’s body as it moves. As a result, it creates a more lifelike experience to have the sprite’s image match the direction that it’s facing.
steps.instructions:
Create a new version of the person sprite that is facing backward.


Duplicate the spriteForward asset, then rename the new asset spriteBackward.


Think about what can remain the same and what is different when the sprite is facing backward. Use the paint tool to edit the sprite’s head by removing the face details and replacing them with hair. Update any clothes on the body of the sprite, too.  


The backwards version of the sprite might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you use the horizontal flip tool to create a left facing sprite image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might different about the sprite’s body when looking from the side?

❓ How should the sprite’s body be modified to create left and right facing versions?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Have the ninja consider what parts of someone’s profile you can see when looking from the side; you likely can only see half of their features (eyes, ears, arms, legs, etc.). Encourage the ninja to tinker with the spacing of the pixels in the sprite’s outline to reflect this.

💡 Once the ninja has modified the sprite’s outline to show the side perspective, have them reorganize the sprite’s clothing to reflect this change.
steps.instructions:
Create new versions of the person sprite that are facing right and left. 


Duplicate the spriteForward asset, then rename the new asset spriteRight.


Use the paint tool to edit the sprite so that it appears to be facing to the right. Think about how the placement of the eyes, arms, and legs might change, and how the different parts might look from the side instead of the front. 


Duplicate the spriteRight asset, then rename the new asset spriteLeft. Use the horizontal flip tool to flip the sprite image to create a left facing sprite image.


The side facing version of the sprite might look like this:

steps.hints: ❓Did you choose a background color not used in the sprite image, so that the sprite will stand out on screen?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What color might be used as the background color, so that the sprite appears clearly on screen?

❓ Why should the sprite’s image be set to the forward facing asset?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that they should use a color not included in the sprite’s image as the background color, so that the sprite appears clearly on screen.

💡 In the next step, the sprite’s image will change when different direction buttons are pressed. The sprite’s current image should be set to the forward-facing image asset so that it appears to be facing the user at the start of the project.
steps.instructions:
Set the scene to display the sprite image on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then set a background color that will allow the sprite to appear clearly on screen.


Then create a sprite with its image set to the spriteForward image asset. Code the sprite to move with direction buttons. 


Click ▶ to see the sprite appear on screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you add on button pressed events for right, left, up, and down buttons so that the sprite image updates to the correct image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image asset should be used in each controller event?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Make sure the ninja has double checked that the image asset matches the direction in each controller event. Prompt them to test out the project by pressing the direction buttons and checking to see if the sprite’s image updates correctly.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need help coding the setImage or controller events.
steps.instructions:
Match the sprite’s image to the direction that it’s facing. 


Code the sprite image to change on right,  left, up, and down button pressed events. Update the sprite image accordingly.


Click ▶ to see the sprite image update depending on the direction button being pressed.

subgroups.title: Create Sprites from Multiple Perspectives
subgroups.introduction: Create multiple points of view for a sprite that can be used to show the direction the sprite is moving or facing.

validationItems.text: Create 4 image assets showing different perspectives of a Player sprite.
Change the Player sprite image depending on the direction button being pressed.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 6 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about creating images that show multiple perspectives of the same sprite and themed sprite packs for projects. You’ll be able to take the strategies you learn in this level to create detailed assets in future projects! Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 6:

badges.title: Package Deal
badges.description: Create a sprite pack that includes different sprite kinds and different perspectives of those sprites, to be used in a project.

badges.title: Covering All My Bases
badges.description: Create pixel art images that show multiple points of view for a sprite: forward, backward, left, and right.

badges.title: Group by Theme
badges.description: Use a specific color palette and theme to create a sprite pack of different sprite kinds.

badges.title: The Gang’s All Here!
badges.description: Create a sprite pack of original pixel art images that includes Player, Collectible, Goal, Enemy, and Projectile sprites.
